identification.summary: Zarya (Russian for 'dawn') is a pro-Russian hacktivist group reported to have emerged in March 2022 as a special-forces-style unit under Killnet and to have become an independent entity known as Zarya in August 2022 [S1][S2]. It is known for DDoS, website defacement and data leaks [S2]. Radware described it in February 2023 as building Mirai variants to enlarge its DDoS botnet [S1].
identification.notes: Sources differ on the Killnet timeline: one account has the unit rejoining Killnet in May 2022 as part of a project called 'Legion', then going independent in August 2022 [S2]; a separate analysis states there are two Zarya groups that both claim links to Killnet [S6]. UAC-0109 is listed as an alias by Malpedia; no CERT-UA publication naming it was found [S8]. 'Zarya Legion' and 'Zarya' are used in the sources as related names; whether they are one cluster is not settled [S2][S6]. SANS suggests the name likely reflects a Cyrillic-style spelling of 'dawn' [S5].

attribution.confidence: Low. No government or vendor attribution to a state organization was found. A leaked US document, as reported by journalists, described Zarya operators showing an FSB-linked handler screenshots of access to a Canadian gas facility [S7]. A Cyberknow analysis says Zarya Legion referenced a relationship with Russian intelligence services; this is one researcher's inference [S6]. Thales judged it unlikely that a group truly associated with Russian armed forces would publicize its actions on a public channel [S3].
attribution.basis: Self-published Telegram claims relayed by Thales and Radware [S1][S3]; leaked-document reporting [S7]; single-analyst assessment [S6]. These are not primary government attribution.

objectives: Disruption, defacement and data leakage against states and organizations seen as opposed to Russia, framed as hacktivism in support of Russia's war in Ukraine [S2][S3]. The group also claimed to have sent members to support Russian forces in Donbass with cyber operations (unverified claim) [S3].

regions: Western states generally ('attacks on the West') [S1]
Canada (alleged gas facility access, per leaked document reporting) [S7]
targeting.notes: Sector list from the group profile in the existing record and secondary summaries [S2]. Most victim claims are self-reported and unverified [S1][S3].

capabilities.summary: DDoS using a botnet; Radware reported the group building Mirai variants to grow it [S1]. Propaganda site 'Zarya - CyberFront' listed links to 48 hacking campaigns and allegedly 655 GB of leaked data (the group's own claim, relayed by Radware); the site and malware were hosted by Akur Group, described as a bulletproof hosting provider [S1]. SANS observed opportunistic scanning for SharePoint servers (CVE-2023-29357 path /_api/web/siteusers) and a defaced host, from infrastructure on the Aeza network (ASN 210644), and characterized the group as using low-hanging-fruit exploits to find defacement targets; SANS judged most attacks would fail even against a vulnerable target [S4][S5]. Researchers questioned whether the group could conduct destructive attacks on critical infrastructure [S7].

campaigns.name: Emergence under Killnet
campaigns.summary: Group reported to emerge as a special-forces-style unit under Killnet command.

campaigns.name: Independence from Killnet
campaigns.summary: Reported to become an independent entity named Zarya (timeline contested across sources).

campaigns.name: Claimed breach of Ukrainian State Logistics Department data
campaigns.summary: Zarya claimed to have stolen databases belonging to the State Logistics Department of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine and published them on its channel; Thales viewed a link to the Donbass-support claim as plausible but unconfirmed.

campaigns.name: Mirai-variant botnet development
campaigns.summary: Radware advisory reports Zarya building Mirai variants to grow its DDoS botnet and hosting its CyberFront site with Akur Group.

campaigns.name: Alleged Canadian gas facility access
campaigns.summary: Reporting on a leaked US document describes Zarya operators showing an FSB-linked handler screenshots of access to a Canadian gas distribution station; researchers doubted capability for destructive attack.

campaigns.name: Possible botnet link to Microsoft DDoS
campaigns.summary: A Cyberknow analysis speculates Anonymous Sudan used a botnet run by Zarya Legion in June 2023 attacks on Microsoft; not confirmed by DOJ or industry reporting found.

campaigns.name: SharePoint scanning and defacement
campaigns.summary: SANS ISC observed pro-Russian scanning for SharePoint CVE-2023-29357 and a defaced host; a follow-up on 2023-12-04 tied the activity to Zarya and Radware's Mirai reporting.

diamond.adversary: Pro-Russian hacktivist collective with Killnet origins; state ties are alleged but unproven [S2][S6][S7].
diamond.capability: DDoS botnet with Mirai variants, defacement, data leaks, opportunistic exploit scanning (SharePoint CVE-2023-29357) [S1][S4][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Akur Group bulletproof hosting for the CyberFront site and malware [S1]; Aeza network (ASN 210644) hosts used for scanning [S5]; Telegram channel for publication of claims [S3].
diamond.victim: Ukrainian state bodies, Western government and service-provider targets, claimed critical infrastructure [S1][S3][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Support for Russia's war in Ukraine; information-effect and visibility goals via public claims [S2][S3].
diamond.technology: Internet-facing unpatched servers (SharePoint), misconfigured or unpatched devices usable for Mirai-type botnets [S1][S5].

gaps: WebFetch could not reach any of the source hosts in this session (DNS failure); content was taken from search-result summaries of Radware, ITWire/Security Solutions Media, Thales, SANS ISC, Cyberknow and Zetter/Security Affairs, and should be verified against the originals.
Radware advisory (Feb 2023) is the primary source for botnet and CyberFront claims but was not opened directly; ITWire and ChannelLife are secondary coverage.
Killnet timeline conflicts between sources (May 2022 rejoin, August 2022 independence, two groups claiming Zarya) [S2][S6].
No Zarya activity found for 2024-2026; current status unknown.
The CERT-UA tracking label UAC-0109 could not be confirmed against a CERT-UA publication [S8].
State sponsorship unverified; the Canadian gas facility and Anonymous Sudan links rest on a leaked-document report and one analyst's inference [S6][S7].
Mandiant's 2022 Killnet report and its 2024 update on Telegram personas (linked to APT44 with high confidence) do not mention Zarya in sources reviewed; do not merge those clusters with Zarya.
Existing record URLs (Mandiant Killnet blog, CYFIRMA, SOCRadar, CIP Ukraine attachment) were not opened and are not cited.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Internet-facing collaboration servers (SharePoint), public web properties and DDoS-exposed services of government and contractors are the terrain this actor touches [S4][S5]. STEP 2: Low sophistication and a record of mostly failed opportunistic attacks limit direct effect, but claimed access and leaks create information-environment effects [S5][S7]. STEP 3: Template is scanning for known CVEs, defacement or data leak, Mirai-style DDoS, then publicity on Telegram and CyberFront [S1][S3][S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued DDoS, defacement and claimed leaks against Ukraine-supporting government and service-provider sites. MDCOA is a state-directed tasking using the group as a deniable front against critical infrastructure, as alleged but unproven in leak reporting [S7]. Candidate indicators: scanning for /_api/web/siteusers, traffic from Aeza ASN 210644, Mirai-variant botnet C2, Telegram claims naming new victims [S1][S4][S5].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track hacktivist Telegram claims separately from confirmed intrusions to avoid overstating effects [S3][S5]. (2) Authorities: reporting is largely open-source; response to DDoS and defacement on DoD-adjacent sites follows normal network defense and law enforcement channels. (3) Mission assurance: patch internet-facing SharePoint and IoT devices and prepare DDoS mitigation for public-facing sites [S1][S4]. (4) Coordination: share indicators such as ASN 210644 activity with DC3/DIB partners and allied CERTs; treat alleged state tasking as unvalidated [S5][S7].
